title: Isolation and characterization of microplastics from human blood samples by confocal RAMAN microscopy
author: Sarabia, Martínez, et al.
materials: - Glass fiber filter membranes (diameter 25 mm, nominal pore size (∼1.6 µm), Whatman; WHA1820025) were pre-treated at 300 °C for 1 h using a Kugelrohr glass oven under vacuum (Model BUCHI 046600). The vacuum environment facilitates the decomposition and removal of polymer-derived contaminants while avoiding thermo-oxidative carbonization, and additionally minimizes exposure to ambient MPs contamination by eliminating the need for carrier gases.

Furthermore, all instances, both in hospital and laboratory settings, where the use of plastic materials was unavoidable were taken into account. steps.title: Decontaminate filter membranes
steps.instruction: Heat glass‑fiber filter membranes (25 mm diameter, ∼1.6 µm pore, Whatman WHA1820025) at 300 °C for 1 h in a Kugelrohr glass oven under vacuum (Model BUCHI 046600).

steps.title: Store pre‑treated filters
steps.instruction: After heating, place the filters on a clean glass Petri dish in the same orientation and keep them ready for use.

steps.title: Filter ultrapure water
steps.instruction: Pass ultrapure water through the pre‑treated glass‑fiber filter membrane before any other use.

steps.title: Clean glassware and autoclave
steps.instruction: Wash all glassware (flasks, Petri dishes, beakers, 15‑ and 40‑mL vials, pipettes, forceps) with running water plus a small amount of 70 % ethanol, rinse with distilled water, rinse again with glass‑filtered water, cover with aluminium foil and sterilise in an autoclave.

steps.title: Prepare contamination‑minimized workspace
steps.instruction: Reduce plastic use, work only with the approved plastic items (21 G × 19 cm butterfly needle with luer adapter, Greiner KG450081; aspirator LSRFXF), wear a 100 % cotton lab coat, clean all surfaces before handling samples, and use a cotton coat instead of synthetic garments.

steps.title: Acquire reference Raman spectra
steps.instruction: Record confocal‑Raman spectra of every plastic item that will contact the sample (gloves, clinical clothing, butterfly needle, Vacutainer cap, etc.) using the same instrument and settings that will be used for the samples; store these spectra as contamination controls.

steps.title: Collect blood samples
steps.instruction: Disinfect the venipuncture site, draw 10 mL of blood into two 5 mL glass Vacutainer tubes (BD Vacutainer 367614) with a safety butterfly needle (21 G × 19 cm, Greiner KG450081), keep the tubes vertical to avoid blood‑cap contact, and transport them at 4 °C.

steps.title: Transfer blood to freezer
steps.instruction: Immediately place each glass Vacutainer tube into a 15 mL glass vial and store the vials at –20 °C until digestion; note that the glass tube may fissure at low temperature but the vial will retain the blood.

steps.title: Prepare digestion solution
steps.instruction: Make a digestion solution (DS) consisting of 10 % (w/v) KOH and 1 % (v/v) Tween‑20 using glass‑filtered ultrapure water; prepare fresh just before use.

steps.title: Digest blood samples
steps.instruction: Defrost the frozen vials, add DS at a ratio of 2 vol DS per 1 vol blood (e.g., 20 mL DS to 10 mL blood) in 40 mL vials, keep the tubes vertical, and incubate at 60 °C for 72 h without shaking. Do not cover the tubes with aluminium foil (reactive with bases).

steps.title: Vacuum membrane filtration
steps.instruction: Assemble a pre‑treated glass‑fiber filter, then filter the entire 30 mL digested sample through it under vacuum.

steps.title: Process filter membrane
steps.instruction: Discard the filtrate, wash the filter with 50 mL glass‑filtered water, neutralise (no vacuum) with 20 mL wash solution (67 % HNO₃ + 1 % Tween‑20) prepared fresh, rinse again with 100 mL glass‑filtered water, dehydrate with 50 mL methanol, and dry at room temperature for 24 h. Keep the dry membrane covered in a glass Petri dish until analysis.

steps.title: Mount filter for Raman
steps.instruction: Place the dried filter on the microscope’s top lid, secure it with double‑sided adhesive tape, cover with the bottom lid, and mark the edge to indicate orientation (do not use pen, pencil or marker).

steps.title: Set up Raman equipment
steps.instruction: Turn on the computer and the 785 nm laser, launch WiRE software, and verify that the laser is linked to the 1200 l mm⁻¹ monochromator.

steps.title: Configure microscope stage
steps.instruction: Press the “Door Release” button, open the microscope door, place the filter (with bottom lid) on the stage, activate the camera view, select the 5× objective on both hardware and WiRE, manually focus the filter surface, and in the Live Video window click “Set Origin” to define (0,0) at the centre of the filter.

steps.title: Calibrate laser
steps.instruction: After a 10‑minute warm‑up, open “Tools → Quick Calibration”, confirm a Raman peak at 520 nm with ~30 000 counts, then close the calibration window.

steps.title: Acquire filter montage image
steps.instruction: In Live Video select “Snap → Montage”, set X and Y limits to –6000 to +6000, close the door, press “Run” to capture the image, and save the file.

steps.title: Capture individual particle images
steps.instruction: In Live Video select “Snap → Single” for each particle of interest and save each image.

steps.title: Perform point‑by‑point Raman measurement
steps.instruction: Lower the stage with the coarse focus knob (sample stays stationary), switch to the 50×L long‑working‑distance objective on both microscope and WiRE, locate and focus the chosen particle, capture a pre‑measurement image, then in Measurements click New → Spectral Acquisition with the following parameters: Grating scan type = Extended; Spectral range = 700–1800 cm⁻¹; Exposure time = 10 s; Laser power = 0.1–1 %; Accumulations = 5–20 (adjust as needed). Press RUN and save the spectrum.

steps.title: Select random analysis points
steps.instruction: Divide the filter into four quadrants, generate random coordinates with an AI tool, and if a generated point lacks a visible particle, choose the nearest particle consistently.

steps.title: Pre‑process raw Raman spectra
steps.instruction: Apply the following processing steps to each spectrum: 1) Min‑Max normalization; 2) Smoothing with a 5th‑order polynomial; 3) Derivative function disabled; 4) Wavenumber window of 50 cm⁻¹; 5) Baseline correction using a 5th‑order polynomial with 25 iterations; 6) Restrict to the 700–1800 cm⁻¹ spectral range.

steps.title: Identify polymers from spectra
steps.instruction: Run the processed spectra through Open Specy with these settings: Spectrum type = Raman; Transformation = none (no baseline); Identification method = Full (search entire library); Correlation threshold = 0.7. Record the polymer match and similarity score.

steps.title: Prepare negative and positive controls
steps.instruction: Create three negative controls: (A) ultrapure water filtered through a glass‑fiber filter; (B) ultrapure water filtered then passed through a butterfly needle; (C) digestion solution prepared with glass‑filtered ultrapure water. Prepare one positive control by filtering a commercial polyethylene standard (REPSOL Alcudio 1940C). Process these controls through the same filtration, washing, drying, and Raman‑analysis steps as the samples to verify absence of artefactual spectra and to confirm detection capability.

description: Using the proposed protocol, MPs were successfully isolated and analysed from human blood samples collected in a clinical setting. To assess potential sources of cross-contamination, several laboratory materials commonly used during sample collection and handling were tested by confocal Raman spectroscopy. The main items illustrated in Fig. 2 include nitrile gloves (Fig. 2A), clinical clothing (Fig. 2B), the butterfly needle cannula (Fig. 2C), and a Vacutainer glass tube (Fig. 2D), with their corresponding Raman spectra shown in panels A′–D′. For each material, representative Raman spectra were obtained and compared with reference data available in Open Specy, a free online platform for spectral analysis, to confirm their polymer composition. These materials were analysed because any contamination derived from them would be visible in the negative controls, thereby ensuring that MPs identified in blood samples could be distinguished from procedural artefacts. Additional items tested, together with their identified polymers and similarity percentages, are summarised in Table 1, which was used to compile a reference library of unavoidable laboratory-derived materials for contamination control. Negative and positive controls were included to evaluate the reliability of the protocol and to rule out potential contamination from laboratory materials or solutions. The negative controls were designed to detect any artefactual signals that might arise during sample handling: ultrapure water filtered through a glass fiber filter (Fig. 3A), ultrapure water filtered through a glass fiber filter and passed through a butterfly needle (Fig. 3B), and digestion solution prepared with glass-filtered ultrapure water (Fig. 3C). Moreover, a positive control was included to validate the performance of the protocol, consisting of a standard commercial polyethylene (REPSOL Alcudio 1940C) (Fig. 3D).
